gloss: The half-title of James Joyce's final masterwork. For seventeen years (1922–1939), Joyce kept the title a strictly guarded secret, referring to the manuscript exclusively as 'Work in Progress'. Only Joyce and his wife Nora Barnacle knew the title until its formal announcement at a Paris publication dinner on Joyce's fifty-seventh birthday (February 2, 1939).

Joyce composed the text in Paris under conditions of near-blindness and failing health, assisted by Samuel Beckett, Stuart Gilbert, Frank Budgen, Eugene Jolas, and Paul Léon. The work synthesizes over sixty languages into a polyphonic dream-fugue.

Bibliographic notice: Published simultaneously on May 4, 1939, by Faber and Faber Ltd (London) and The Viking Press (New York). A deluxe signed limited edition of 428 copies (numbered and signed by Joyce) was printed on English handmade paper by R. MacLehose & Co. Ltd. at The University Press, Glasgow.

gloss: The introduction of the artist-figure. Modeled on Jim the Bowman (a known forger) and Joyce himself, he represents the creative but transgressive son.
Introduces Shem, Joyce's self-portrait as the exiled, misunderstood avant-garde artist. He is the polar opposite of his brother Shaun.
Shem embodies introversion, artistic exile, and failure, standing in stark contrast to Shaun's extroversion, political success, and public conformity.
The dichotomy between the brothers draws heavily on Giordano Bruno's theory of the coincidence of contraries, essential to the Wake's structure.
Shem's role as the creative but socially despised artist highlights Joyce's own fraught relationship with Irish politics and society.
The devastating self-portrait begins. Joyce strips away romantic notions of the artist, presenting Shem as a trickster and a plagiarist rather than a genius.
Reflects Joyce's self-imposed exile in Europe to write freely, juxtaposed against the superficial acclaim of those who stayed behind.
The entire chapter is narrated by a hostile 'Shaunish' voice, a brilliant ironic device Joyce uses to defend himself by mocking his critics.
The narrator's vehement attacks on Shem's character, hygiene, and morals catalogue every criticism leveled against Joyce's own work.
By adopting the persona of his fiercest detractors, Joyce neutralizes their attacks, turning their vitriol into the substance of his art.
A pun on Daedalus 'forging' the uncreated conscience of his race, now degraded to literal criminal forgery. Shem creates art by stealing and twisting existing texts.
The ultimate act of self-consumption and solipsism. Shem uses his own body as parchment, reflecting Joyce's deeply autobiographical and physically taxing writing process.
A shocking grotesque image. It suggests that literature is produced from the base waste of the author's life, echoing the hen's discovery in the midden heap.
Shem's defiance of orthodox religion. His writing is presented as an anti-sacrament, a dark parody of the Word made flesh.
The physical and spiritual isolation of the artist. Shem is cast out from normal society, a clear parallel to Joyce's self-imposed exile in Europe.
A reference to Joyce's failing eyesight and Shem's inward focus. He ignores external reality to mine the depths of his own internal darkness.

gloss: Structural overview of Book III. gloss: Introduction of the aggressive, bureaucratic twin in his full public persona, contrasting with the introverted Shem.
Shaun's journey down the river contrasts with ALP's upstream flow, emphasizing his role as a passive vehicle moving with the current.
Shaun's literal and symbolic journey through the fluid female element (ALP), presenting himself as a messianic arrival.
The vessel is a Guinness barrel, aligning Shaun with commerce, stout, and the material economy of Dublin, in stark contrast to Shem's artistry.
An ironic reference to Diogenes the Cynic; unlike the philosopher who rejected wealth, Shaun is deeply materialistic while confined to his tub.
The vessel of Shaun's arrival, evoking both a Guinness barrel and the infant Moses' basket, satirizing his claims to salvation.
Mamalujo interrogates the floating postman with fourteen specific questions, acting as inquisitors seeking the true meaning of the letter.
Shaun's dogmatic and hypocritical address to the people, parodying rigid religious instruction and moralizing rhetoric.
During the interrogation, Shaun remains characteristically pompous and evasive, refusing to admit his fundamental ignorance of the letter's contents.
Emphasizes Shaun's materialism and gluttony, physically contrasting with the starving artist archetype of his brother Shem.
Shaun takes the opportunity to violently criticize his brother Shem, reinforcing the dichotomy of the conventional bourgeois versus the exiled artist.
Shaun's tragedy is that he is merely the courier of the Wake's profound message, physically transporting a truth he is incapable of comprehending.
Shaun's self-definition entirely in opposition to his brother, highlighting the adversarial duality at the core of the Wake's fraternal conflict.
The physical instability of the barrel foreshadows Shaun's eventual loss of balance and subsequent disappearance backwards at the chapter's end.
The authoritative, Latinate tone Shaun adopts to assert dominance, mocking institutional church edicts and infallibility.
Shaun's voice projected as a modern mass-media broadcast, showing his affinity for public relations over genuine artistic creation.
